title: “MY GOD, MY GOD, WHY HAVE YOU FORSAKEN ME?” — THE CRY FROM THE CROSS THAT WAS REALLY ABOUT YOU
paragraphs:
“MY GOD, MY GOD, WHY HAVE YOU FORSAKEN ME?” — THE CRY FROM THE CROSS THAT WAS REALLY ABOUT YOU
Jesus was not losing His faith. He was carrying sinners through the darkest hour of the Gospel—and the Psalm behind His cry changes how you hear Calvary forever.
There are words Jesus spoke from the cross that almost everyone recognizes.
But there are four words hiding inside them that many people have never really allowed themselves to feel:
Why have You forsaken Me?
Think about that.
This is Jesus.
The One who touched lepers when everyone else backed away.
The One who forgave adulterers, welcomed sinners, confronted hypocrites, opened blind eyes, and called dead men out of graves.
The One who taught His disciples to trust the Father.
Now He is hanging between earth and sky...
bleeding.
mocked.
rejected.
surrounded by people waiting for Him to die.
And suddenly, out of the darkness, comes a scream.
Matthew records the words this way:
“Ἠλί Ἠλί λεμὰ σαβαχθανί”
Ēli, Ēli, lema sabachthani?
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
Matthew 27:46.
Mark preserves the opening slightly differently:
“Ἐλωΐ Ἐλωΐ λεμὰ σαβαχθανί”
Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?
The cry preserves Semitic wording in the Greek Gospel text. And it points directly backward to words Israel had already been praying for centuries.
Psalm 22.
That matters enormously.
Because Jesus was not inventing a sentence in His agony.
He was reaching into Scripture.
Psalm 22 begins in Hebrew:
אֵלִי אֵלִי לָמָה עֲזַבְתָּנִי
Eli, Eli, lamah azavtani?
“My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?”
Psalm 22:1.
Jesus was dying with Scripture on His lips.
But don't move past that too quickly.
Because knowing that Jesus was quoting Psalm 22 does not make His suffering pretend.
This was not Jesus performing religious theater for the crowd.
The nails were real.
The thirst was real.
The humiliation was real.
The darkness was real.
The death was real.
And His cry was real.
This is where Calvary becomes almost unbearable to look at.
The sinless Son of God had willingly stepped into the place of sinners.
Paul writes:
2 Corinthians 5:21.
Peter says Christ “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God.”
1 Peter 3:18.
Isaiah had seen the shadow of this suffering centuries earlier:
“He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities.”
Isaiah 53:5.
Do you see what is happening?
Jesus did not die because He had sinned.
He died for sinners.
He did not stand condemned because evil had finally defeated Him.
He willingly gave Himself as the spotless sacrifice through whom guilty people could be reconciled to God.
That means the question of the cross eventually reaches your name.
And mine.
Because sin becomes easy to tolerate when we only call it a “mistake.”
We hide pride behind personality.
We rename lust as weakness.
We disguise bitterness as boundaries.
We call greed ambition.
We call gossip concern.
We call compromise complexity.
We learn Christian vocabulary while quietly protecting the very things Jesus calls us to surrender.
We can sing worship songs on Sunday and feed secret addictions on Monday.
We can post Bible verses while refusing to forgive someone.
We can tell everybody that God is good while privately wondering why He allowed our lives to hurt this badly.
Some people reading this know exactly what hiding feels like.
You smile in photographs.
You answer, “I’m fine.”
You keep serving.
Keep working.
Keep posting.
Keep laughing.
Keep showing up.
But somewhere behind the version of you everybody sees is another person whispering:
“God... where are You?”
Maybe someone abandoned you.
Maybe your marriage shattered.
Maybe the person you prayed for still died.
Maybe the child you raised walked away from God.
Maybe you begged for healing and the diagnosis remained.
Maybe you promised Jesus you would never return to that sin...
and then you did.
Again.
And now shame has convinced you that God must be tired of you.
That is why the cry from Calvary reaches so deeply into wounded people.
Jesus entered suffering so completely that Christianity cannot dismiss human anguish with shallow slogans.
At the cross, we do not meet a Savior unfamiliar with pain.
We meet the Man of Sorrows.
But something even greater is happening.
Jesus' words open Psalm 22.
And when you read the Psalm beside the crucifixion accounts, the parallels are striking.
The sufferer is mocked.
People ridicule his trust in God.
His suffering becomes physically devastating.
His garments are divided.
Lots are cast for his clothing.
Then look at Calvary.
Jesus is mocked.
His trust in God becomes part of the mockery.
His garments are divided.
Lots are cast.
Matthew's passion narrative repeatedly echoes the language and imagery of Psalm 22.
The crucified Jesus stands inside the story that Psalm 22 had already given God's people.
Yet Psalm 22 does something many people miss.
It does not end where it begins.
It begins with:
“Why have You forsaken me?”
But suffering does not get the final sentence.
Later the Psalm declares that God has heard the afflicted one's cry.
Then the horizon becomes enormous.
The nations are brought into view.
People yet unborn will hear what God has done.
The Psalm moves from abandonment and agony toward vindication, worship, proclamation, and worldwide hope.
In other words...
Jesus chose the opening words of a Psalm whose darkness does not win.
And neither would the darkness of Golgotha.
This is why we have to be careful when explaining the cry of Jesus.
Christians sometimes say that the Father simply stopped loving the Son, or that the Trinity somehow broke apart at Calvary.
Scripture does not require us to say that.
The eternal Father, Son, and Holy Spirit did not cease to be the triune God.
The divine nature of the Son did not suddenly dissolve.
The Trinity was not destroyed for three hours.
Yet neither should we empty Jesus' cry of its terrible weight.
The Son truly suffered.
He truly died.
He truly bore our sins.
He truly endured the judgment associated with our rebellion as our representative and substitute.
Galatians says:
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.”
Galatians 3:13.
Peter writes:
1 Peter 2:24.
And perhaps one of the most beautiful explanations comes from the same apostle:
“Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous...”
Why?
“...that he might bring us to God.”
1 Peter 3:18.
There it is.
To bring us to God.
That is the heart of the cross.
Jesus did not suffer so you could become slightly more religious.
He did not die so you could decorate your life with inspirational Christian quotations while remaining lord of your own heart.
He did not rise again merely to improve your mood.
He came to reconcile rebels to God.
To forgive sinners.
To break the dominion of sin.
To give eternal life.
To make enemies children.
To bring the lost home.
And suddenly the scandal becomes grace.
The innocent One stands where the guilty belonged.
The King wears thorns.
The Creator is mocked by creatures.
The hands through whom creation came are stretched upon wood.
The One without sin bears the sins of others.
And the grave receives Someone it cannot keep.
That is Christianity.
Not humanity climbing toward God.
God coming for humanity in Jesus Christ.
Not good people earning heaven.
Sinners receiving mercy through a crucified and risen Savior.
Not pretending your past never happened.
Redemption.
This is why our message remains:
Maybe your story has scandal in it.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe your worst chapter has your fingerprints all over it.
Maybe someone else's sin shattered you.
Maybe you have spent years trying to outrun what happened.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more than we wanted to admit.
But the cross also proves something else:
God's grace reaches farther than repentant sinners ever dared to hope.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending evil was good.
He rewrites everything through redemption.
Peter denied Him.
Christ restored Peter.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Christ transformed Paul into a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The thief beside Jesus could not climb down from his cross and rebuild his reputation.
He could not spend twenty years proving himself.
He could not repay everybody.
He had nothing left to offer except a desperate appeal to the King dying beside him.
And grace met him there.
Maybe that is what someone reading this needs to understand.
You do not need to clean yourself enough to make Jesus willing to save you.
You come because you cannot save yourself.
You repent.
You believe.
You surrender your excuses.
You stop negotiating with the sin that is destroying you.
And you throw yourself upon the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Grace is free to us.
It was not cheap to Him.
Look again at the cross.
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
And then remember what comes afterward.
“It is finished.”
The cry of anguish was not the final word.
The tomb was not the final word.
Rome was not the final word.
The religious leaders were not the final word.
Your sin does not have to have the final word either.
Jesus does.
Three days later, the stone could not hold the Author of life.
Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead.
The crucified Messiah became the proclaimed risen Lord.
And because He lives, forgiveness is not wishful thinking.
Grace is not positive thinking.
Redemption is not religious poetry.
The Gospel announces that Christ died for sins, was buried, and was raised.
So now this article has to stop being merely about theology.
It has to become personal.
What are you hiding?
What have you refused to surrender?
What wound has become your identity?
What sin have you renamed so you can keep it?
What resentment are you feeding?
What secret would terrify you if everybody discovered it?
What happened to the person who once prayed with fire?
Where did you become cold?
Where did you stop trusting?
Where did following Jesus become merely looking Christian?
Nobody here can stop you.
But scrolling cannot silence the question forever:
What will you do with Jesus Christ?
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't manufacture a spiritual performance.
Be honest before God.
Someone reading beneath this article may need the evidence of grace written in your story.
Don't underestimate what one honest testimony can do.
And don't keep this message trapped on this page.
There may be somebody on your Facebook friends list who would never walk into a church this week but would read something you shared at 1:17 in the morning.
Someone fighting addiction.
Someone contemplating giving up.
Someone angry with God.
Someone drowning in shame.
Someone who thinks Christianity has nothing left to say to them.
Someone who desperately needs to hear that Jesus Christ still receives repentant sinners.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
It doesn't.
It cannot.
But if the Gospel has given you something worth proclaiming, using your influence to put Christ before another human being can become an act of witness.
There may come a night when you need to return to the truth that your feelings are not the final authority over whether God is faithful.
And invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even unbelievers—to follow too.
Not to buy God's approval.
Not to earn salvation.
Not to prove you love Jesus.
Christ's finished work cannot be purchased.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come to Christ.
Bring Him the sin.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the questions.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the secret chapter.
Bring Him the shattered pieces.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus Christ can redeem a sinner's tomorrow.
At Calvary, the world saw scandal.
Heaven was accomplishing redemption.
The cross looked like defeat.
Sunday revealed victory.
The condemned thief saw a dying man and called Him King.
The centurion watched Him die and recognized something extraordinary.
The disciples thought everything had ended.
God was writing resurrection into the next chapter.
And perhaps that is why those terrifying words still echo across two thousand years:
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
Because Jesus entered the darkness sinners deserved so that those who belong to Him would never have to face judgment without a Savior.
Because Psalm 22 begins with anguish but moves toward proclamation.
Because Good Friday leads toward resurrection morning.
Because shame does not have to become your identity.
Because your worst chapter does not have authority to write your ending.
Because there is still blood-bought mercy for repentant sinners.
Still forgiveness.
Still a cross.
Still an empty tomb.
Still a risen King.
Still Jesus.
And comment something honest—not something impressive.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“I’m still fighting.”
“Pray for me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
Or simply tell us what Jesus has brought you through.
Because somewhere beneath your comment may be a stranger wondering whether grace could possibly reach someone like them.
Your story might whisper the answer.
The cry from the cross sounded like the end—but in the hands of Jesus, even the darkest sentence can become the doorway to resurrection.
